verses.note: The goal of the feeding is not a benefit received but a union: Christ in the believer and the believer in Christ. Every tradition that reads 6:53-58, sacramentally or not, finds here the heart of the passage, and the vine of 15:4-7 develops it.
The sheep's knowledge of Christ is modeled on the Son's knowledge of the Father. Belonging to Christ is not a transaction but a shared life, the union Jesus will pray for in 17:21-23.

Both promises depend on believing eis eme, ‘into me’. Life is not a benefit Jesus hands over at a distance; it is shared by those joined to him, which is why he can promise that the believer will never finally die.
‘Where I am, there my servant will also be’ describes discipleship as sharing Jesus' place: his road to death now, and his presence with the Father afterward (14:3, 17:24).

To have a part with Jesus is to share his life and destiny, and the condition is being washed by him. Union with Christ begins with receiving his service, which is humbling for those who would rather serve than be served.

The union of believers with Christ is patterned on the union of the Son with the Father, though it is not identical to it: the disciples are in the Son, and he in them, by grace and not by nature. The verse is one of the foundations of the doctrine that believers share Christ's life, which Paul expresses as Christ living in me (Galatians 2:20).

The future dwelling with God (verse 2) and the present dwelling of God with the believer (verse 23) use the same word. Union with Christ is not only the believer's place in God's house but God's home in the believer, which the rest of the New Testament describes as the dwelling of Christ in the heart by faith (Ephesians 3:17) and the church as God's temple (2 Corinthians 6:16).

The union of the disciple with Christ mirrors the Son's dependence on the Father. As the Son does nothing from himself but what he sees the Father doing (5:19), the branch bears nothing from itself. Union with Christ is not a technique but a dependence, and the command to remain is a command to keep receiving.

The union is mutual (I in him, he in me) and fruitful. Nothing in the verse suggests that the branch contributes life to the vine; everything the branch bears it has received, which is why every Christian tradition has used this verse to say that good works flow from grace.

Jesus' own joy, the joy of the Son in the Father's love, is given to those who remain in him. Joy in this chapter is not a mood produced by circumstances but a share in Christ's own life, and the next chapter will promise a joy no one can take away (16:22).

The prayer ends where the discourse on the vine began: Christ in his people. The union that 15:4-5 described as branches remaining in the vine is here the Son's presence in believers, carrying the Father's love with it.

For the first time Jesus calls the disciples ‘my brothers’. Through his death and rising they share his relationship to the Father, which fulfills 1:12, those who receive him become children of God. The repeated possessives keep a distinction: he is Son by nature and they are children by grace (Hebrews 2:11-12).

Believers are saved ‘in his life’: the risen Christ's life is the sphere in which they live and the power that keeps them. Paul will develop this in 6:4-11, where the baptized share Christ's death and resurrection life.
People belong to one of two heads. What each head did determines the standing of those who belong to him, which is why being ‘in Christ’, the theme of chapters 6-8, is everything for Paul.

‘Into Christ Jesus’ is the language of union with Christ, the idea that runs beneath the whole chapter. What happened to Christ is counted as having happened to those joined to him, which is why his death to sin can be called theirs.

‘United’ (literally ‘grown together’) is one of Paul's strongest images of union with Christ. The believer's life is organically joined to his, so that his death and resurrection become the shape of theirs.
‘In Christ Jesus’ is the heart of Paul's account of salvation. The believer is dead to sin and alive to God not in himself but in Christ, which is why the reckoning rests on fact rather than feeling.

Union with Christ is pictured as marriage. Believers are joined to the risen Christ as a wife to a husband, a theme Paul develops in 2 Corinthians 11:2 and Ephesians 5:25-32, and which the prophets used for God and Israel (Hosea 2:19-20).
‘In Christ Jesus’ is the reason for the verdict. The sentence that fell on Christ in his death (verse 3) cannot fall again on those who are joined to him.
Those who belong to Christ share his destiny because they share his life. The image of firstfruits and harvest makes the bond organic: the rest of the crop follows because it is the same crop.
Belonging to Christ means taking on his likeness, begun now (2 Corinthians 3:18) and completed in the resurrection body (Philippians 3:21, 1 John 3:2).

The believer's death to the law happens in union with Christ's death. Paul speaks of it as his own experience: what happened to Christ on the cross happened to him, so that his relationship to the law as a way of righteousness is over.

Union with Christ is here both death and life: the believer has died with him and Christ lives in the believer. The Christian life is not a self-improvement project but the life of Christ lived out in a human body by faith.
The one seed becomes many by incorporation. Those who are ‘in Christ’ are counted in the singular seed, which is how Paul can say both that the seed is Christ and that believers are the seed.
Sonship is ‘in Christ Jesus’. Believers are God's children because they are joined to the Son, and they share his status as heir.
To be clothed with Christ is to be so identified with him that God sees his children in his Son. The image goes beyond imitation: believers wear Christ's identity.
Every blessing is ‘in Christ’. The phrase ‘in Christ’ or ‘in him’ occurs about eleven times in verses 3 to 14; nothing is given to believers apart from their union with him.

The repeated ‘with Christ’ and ‘in Christ Jesus’ make union with Christ the ground of salvation. What happened to him (resurrection and enthronement) is counted as having happened to those joined to him, so their standing is as secure as his.
Christ is so joined to his people that their afflictions can be called his (Acts 9:4). The verse assumes the union with Christ that the hymn has just described.
Believers are ‘partners of Christ’, sharing in him and in his kingdom. The union is real and already begun, which is why the call to hold fast is so serious.
The way into God's presence is Christ himself, his flesh given in death and his life as the ‘living’ way. To draw near to God is to go where he has gone, through him.
